title: "Twists, Wrenches, and the Screw Axis"

# Twists, Wrenches, and the Screw Axis {#sec-screw}

::: {.callout-note}

A screw axis combines rotation and translation into a single motion, the way a
corkscrew simultaneously spins and advances. Nearly every rigid-body motion in
3D can be described as a screw: rotating around some axis while sliding along it.
This seemingly obscure observation turns out to be one of the most powerful ideas
in robotics, reducing complex spatial motions to a single geometric object.
:::

## The Unified $4 \times 4$ Transform SE(3)


We established that tracking a physical object requires two elements: its translation vector $p \in \Reals^3$ and its $3 \times 3$ Rotation Matrix $R \in \SO$. 

If a robot moves its arm to a new location, how do we mathematically calculate the new coordinates of a point attached to that arm? We have to compute an algebraically cumbersome operation: first multiply by the Rotation Matrix $R$ and then add the translation vector $p$ separately. 

$$
\bm{x}_{mapped} = R\bm{x}_{\text{body}} + p
$$

This destroys our hope of treating control as a clean, unified geometry. 

To unify translation and rotation into a single, flawless algebraic operation, mathematicians embed the $3 \times 3$ matrix and the $1 \times 3$ vector into a magnificent $4 \times 4$ matrix.


::: {.callout-note}

  By appending a row of zeros and a single '1' to the bottom, we define the **Homogeneous Transformation Matrix** $\bm{T}$:
  
$$
T = \begin{bmatrix} R & p  \bm{0} & 1 \end{bmatrix} \in \Reals^{4 \times 4}
$$

  The continuous Space of all valid Transformation Matrices mapping rigid body movement is called the **Special Euclidean Group in 3 Dimensions**, denoted as $\SE$.

:::


This transforms $\bm{x}_{mapped} = R\bm{x} + p$ into entirely unified multiplication $\bm{x}_{new} = T \times \bm{x}_{old}$ by defining points as $\bm{x}_{homo} = [x, y, z, 1]^T$. 

This is the central nervous system of physics simulations: MuJoCo, game engines (Unreal), and modern control theory map everything back to these $4 \times 4$ coordinates. 


## Chasles' Theorem and the Screw Axis


If $T \in \SE$ defines the complete layout of a rigid body in space, what is the *velocity* of that body as it moves? 

Just as translation and rotation were unified into $T$, linear velocity $v \in \Reals^3$ and singular angular velocity $\omega \in \Reals^3$ are unified into a 6-dimensional **Spatial Velocity** vector.

According to French mathematician Michel Chasles (1830), any complex movement of a rigid body floating in space?a gymnast twisting and flipping through the air concurrently?can be expressed geometrically as movement along a **single, specific mathematical axis** passing through space.


::: {.callout-note}

  Think of a literal screw going into wood. As the screw turns along an axis (pitching rotation), it simultaneously plunges forward along that precise identical axis (linear translation). 
  
  Mathematically, a chaotic tumbling body is just spinning around a single invisible straight line in space (Rotation) while simultaneously sliding down that very same line (Translation).

:::


A **Screw Axis** $\screw$ contains the full geometric map of this line. Specifically it is defined by:
1. An origin point $\bm{q}$ in Space that the line passes through.
2. A direction unit vector $\hat{\bm{s}}$ defining the line.
3. The *Pitch* $h$, which defines the ratio of translation speed to rotation speed (how "steep" the threads of the virtual screw are).

::: {.callout-note}
## Pitch, formally

For a screw motion with angular part $\bm{\omega}$ and linear (origin) velocity $\bm{v}$, the pitch is the ratio of translation along $\hat{\bm{s}} = \bm{\omega}/\|\bm{\omega}\|$ to rotation about that axis:
$$ h = \frac{\bm{v} \cdot \hat{\bm{s}}}{\|\bm{\omega}\|} \quad \text{(units: length/radian, with } \|\bm{\omega}\| > 0\text{).} $$

Two limiting cases matter in practice:

- **Pure rotation** ($\bm{\omega} \neq 0$, axis passes through the origin with no translation along $\hat{\bm{s}}$): $h = 0$.
- **Pure translation** ($\bm{\omega} = 0$): $h = \infty$. The "axis" is degenerate (a direction only), and the canonical unit screw becomes $\screw = [\bm{0};\, \hat{\bm{v}}]$.

Equivalently, any 6-vector $[\bm{\omega};\, \bm{v}]$ with $\bm{\omega} \neq 0$ decomposes as a screw axis at point $\bm{q} = (\bm{\omega} \times \bm{v})/\|\bm{\omega}\|^2$ with direction $\hat{\bm{s}} = \bm{\omega}/\|\bm{\omega}\|$ and pitch $h = (\bm{\omega} \cdot \bm{v})/\|\bm{\omega}\|^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Plücker Coordinates for a Line

A line $\ell$ in $\Reals^3$ passing through point $\bm{q}$ with unit direction $\hat{\bm{s}}$ has **Plücker coordinates**
$$ \bm{L} = \begin{bmatrix} \hat{\bm{s}}  \hat{\bm{s}} \times \bm{q} \end{bmatrix} \in \Reals^6. $$
The second triple (the *moment* of the line about the origin) is invariant to the choice of $\bm{q}$ along $\ell$. Plücker coordinates give the minimal frame-independent representation of a line and underlie the Ad / Ad$^{-T}$ duality used to transport twists and wrenches between frames (see §The Spatial Wrench below).
:::


### The Spatial Twist ($\twist$)


If the Screw Axis $\screw$ is the geometric "thread," the **Twist** $\twist \in \Reals^6$ is the velocity at which the body physically slides along and spins around that thread.


$$
\twist = \begin{bmatrix} \omega  v \end{bmatrix} = \screw \dot{\theta}
$$


Where $\dot{\theta}$ is the speed the body moves along the Screw. A Twist completely unifies angular $\omega$ and linear $v$ velocity into a single variable. This perfectly maps the derivative (speed) of the Configuration Space map $\configspace$ we created earlier.

::: {.callout-important}
## Spatial 6-Vector Ordering

Throughout *The Geometry of Motion*, spatial 6-vectors are ordered **(angular ; linear)**: $\twist = [\bm{\omega};\, \bm{v}]$, $\wrench = [\bm{m};\, \bm{f}]$, $\screw = [\hat{\bm{s}};\, \hat{\bm{s}}\times\bm{q} + h\hat{\bm{s}}]$. This matches Lynch & Park [@lynch2017modern], MuJoCo, and Pinocchio. Featherstone [@featherstone2008rigid] uses the opposite ordering **(linear ; angular)**; when interoperating with Featherstone-style code, swap the two halves. We note this convention once here and enforce it in every subsequent chapter.
:::


### The Spatial Wrench ($\wrench$)


Just as velocity is unified into Twists along a Screw Axis ($\twist \in \Reals^6$), Newton's physical forces are unified by the exact same geometry. 

Torques ($m \in \Reals^3$) and linear pushes ($f \in \Reals^3$) are merged into a 6-Dimensional **Wrench** $\wrench$, which operates on the body along that same mathematical Screw Axis.


$$
\wrench = \begin{bmatrix} m  f \end{bmatrix} \in \Reals^6
$$


When modeling the physics engines throughout *Tangent-Space Methods*, every mechanical coupling, robotic joint, actuator limit, and contact force is calculated exclusively using $6D$ Spatial Twists and Wrenches operating in $\se$.

::: {.callout-note}
## Twist?Wrench Duality and Power

Twists live in the Lie algebra $\se$; wrenches live in its dual $\se^*$. The natural pairing between them,
$$ P = \wrench^T \twist = \bm{m} \cdot \bm{\omega} + \bm{f} \cdot \bm{v}, $$
is the instantaneous **mechanical power** delivered by $\wrench$ to a body whose spatial velocity is $\twist$. Because power is frame-independent, twists and wrenches transform by *different* maps under change of frame?missing this distinction is a common source of sign and magnitude errors in inverse dynamics.
:::

## Adjoint (Ad) and Lie-Bracket (ad) Operators

Two matrix operators appear everywhere in the recursive algorithms of the coming chapters, and both are introduced here so that later chapters can cite them without fanfare.

For a homogeneous transform $T = \begin{bmatrix} R & \bm{p}  \bm{0} & 1 \end{bmatrix} \in \SE$, the **Adjoint map** $\operatorname{Ad}_T : \se \to \se$ transports twists between frames:

$$
\operatorname{Ad}_T = \begin{bmatrix} R & \bm{0}  [\bm{p}]_\times R & R \end{bmatrix} \in \Reals^{6 \times 6}.
$$


For a twist $\twist = [\bm{\omega};\, \bm{v}] \in \se$, the **Lie-bracket matrix form** $\operatorname{ad}_\twist : \se \to \se$ is

$$
\operatorname{ad}_\twist = \begin{bmatrix} [\bm{\omega}]_\times & \bm{0}  [\bm{v}]_\times & [\bm{\omega}]_\times \end{bmatrix} \in \Reals^{6 \times 6}.
$$


Under change of frame, **twists transform with Ad**, whereas **wrenches transform with its inverse-transpose** (which is how power stays invariant):
$$
\twist_A = \operatorname{Ad}_{T_{AB}}\, \twist_B, \qquad
\wrench_A = \operatorname{Ad}_{T_{AB}}^{-T}\, \wrench_B.
$$

These operators are used immediately in @sec-rnea (RNEA / ABA velocity and wrench recursion) and @sec-poe (Product of Exponentials). The particular block structure above is the Lynch & Park §3.3 convention; Featherstone's $[\bm{v};\, \bm{\omega}]$ ordering produces block-swapped versions of the same operators.

We now finally possess the mathematical primer necessary to leave the stationary world behind, map the configuration of physical bodies flawlessly via $SE(3)$, understand their rotational matrices, and track their trajectories as infinitesimally precise 6D vectors. The fundamental mathematics are established.

We may now proceed to Volume I: The Geometry of those spaces.

## Exercises {#sec-screw-exercises}

**5.1 (Computational)** For a revolute joint at $\bm{q}=(1,0,0)$ spinning about $\hat{z}$, write the unit screw $\screw=(\hat{\bm{\omega}};\bm{v})$. Verify $\bm{v} = -\hat{\bm{\omega}} 	imes \bm{q}$.

**5.2 (Conceptual)** What is the pitch of a pure revolute joint? A pure prismatic joint? Give a physical example with nonzero finite pitch.

**5.3 (Computational)** Compute instantaneous power $P=\wrench^T	wist$ and verify it is frame-independent by transforming to a shifted frame and recomputing. See [@lynch2017modern, §3.3] and [@featherstone2008rigid, Ch. 2].

**5.4 (Conceptual)** Prove that wrenches transform by $\operatorname{Ad}_T^{-T}$ (not $\operatorname{Ad}_T$) in order to keep the power pairing $\wrench^T	wist$ frame-invariant.
